steps.narration: At the end of the blue level, the tribes of the world have become nations. Here we open one of them, the United States, and look inside its economy. The logic does not change. In the biosphere, higher organisms live on the calories of the ones beneath them. In an economy, the top companies build their businesses on other businesses, on infrastructure, and on basic subsistence work, and all of it stands on a foundation of government. It is a food chain made of money. The same arrow of cause and effect that carried us from the first stars to the first cities now runs through paychecks, taxes and markets. Nothing here is separate from what came before. It is the newest layer of the same chain.

The road of American lives since nineteen forty-six and the economy share a single time axis, so a year on the wave stands beside the same year on the road. At the present moment, the cross-section of the road opens into a wave. Each rib behind the crest is one year of the economy, and the wave widens as real output grows. The crest is the year you are looking at. One honest note before we go on: this is a model, built on public accounts and on assumptions. Treat it as a way of seeing, not a measurement.

Beneath the whole landscape lies the bedrock: government. Every society stands on a different foundation, and in the United States it is a constitutional federal democracy. The pillars you see are sized by public outlays, what the government spends. Watch taxes fall into the bedrock from every household, and watch benefits rise back out of it to the people who receive them. Nothing on the hills above could stand without it. Like the sunlight at the base of a food chain, it is the layer that everything else presumes.

On the bedrock, the economy rises in layers, each standing on the ones beneath it. At the foot are raw materials and the subsistence infrastructure people need simply to live. Above that, manufacturing and infrastructure. Then services, and at the top, technology. Each industry is a ridge, and its width is its share of the value the economy adds. Height here is an order of dependence, not of importance. As in the food chain, the top cannot exist without everything underneath it, feeding it.

Companies live on these ridges the way people live on the road. There are seventy-five of them here. Each is born on its industry's ridge, rises and falls with its market value, and then meets its fate. Some fail and fall to the ground. Some are bought and merge into their buyer. Some survive all the way to the crest. Their color tells you how they sell: by meeting real needs, by manufactured want, or by fear. Watch them flicker into being and go out, like stars with short lives.

Follow a dollar to any market on these hills and watch it split. Wages run back down to the people who did the work. Taxes fall to the bedrock. What remains, the surplus, climbs upward into gold halos above the summits, and into the rings of owners around the top firms: the golden circles. Like the top of a food chain, they live on what flows up from everything below. And they are few, by the same arithmetic that makes falcons rarer than moths.

Now the people. On this landscape, class is altitude. Each group lives on the slope of whatever pays them, placed as close as possible to its source of value: an employer's industry, the government, or family wealth. The out of work sit on the valley floor. The richest float above it all. Between them, every rung of a society is laid out as height, and you can read a nation's hierarchy the way you would read a mountain range.

Money moves across the landscape in rivers of two colors. Rose is desire. Ice is fear. Spending runs from households down to each industry's market, colored by the motive behind it. Saving leaves over the crest into the future, as capital that builds what comes next. Debt arrives from the future: spending drawn from income not yet earned. Watch where the rivers run and you see what a people wants, and what it is afraid of, written in the shape of its own money.

Zoom all the way down to one person. Where they stand on this hillside is where they stand in the social market: the slope that pays them, the rung they occupy, and the people around them. In the universe graph, this person was one thin line inside a stream. Here you can see the ground beneath their feet. Remember that they are synthetic. Each one stands in for many real people, not for anyone you could look up. The model is about the pattern, not the person.

Now step inside that person's mind. Five drives of desire, and five drives of fear, weighed by reason into a choice. Desire pulls toward the hills that pay and the things that please. Fear pushes away from debt, from loss, from scarcity. Every river you saw on the landscape begins here, in decisions like this one, made over and over by millions of minds. It is a simplified mind, but the tug of war it shows is real, and it is as old as the first animal that chose between food and danger.

No one decides alone. Every encounter between two people is a prisoner's dilemma: cooperate, or defect and try to take more. Over many rounds, one of the most successful strategies is called tit for tat. It opens kindly. It copies whatever its partner did last. It retaliates when cheated, and it forgives the moment the other side cooperates again. Here, the payoffs from all those encounters accumulate over time as wealth. Simple rules, repeated, and a society's fortunes grow out of them.

This is the ladder: one life's path across the landscape over time. Watch it climb and fall between the rungs. A new job can lift it. Marriage can join two paths. Children cost money and time. Debt can pull it down, or help it climb. Beside it, compare where this person ended up with the rung their parents stood on. Anyone can move up or down this hillside. The questions that matter are how, and what it costs, and who else was moving at the same time.

Groups play the same game as individuals. Companies, classes and whole tribes meet one another again and again, and each time they choose to cooperate or to defect. Watch cooperation, retaliation and forgiveness play out between them. Coalitions form wherever cooperating keeps paying, and break where it stops. It is the same logic that held the first human tribes together on the grasslands, now playing out on a landscape of money.

Pull back to the wave. This economy is the newest layer of the same chain of causes that began with the Big Bang: matter, then life, then people, and now the systems people build on one another. It is a model, with assumptions built into it, and the assumptions deserve to be questioned. But its shape follows the shape of everything before it: layers standing on layers, each living on what flows up from below, all of it moving one way through time. You are somewhere on this hillside. Beneath you stand the bedrock, the ridges, the sunlight and the stars. Ahead of you is the next rib of the wave, not yet drawn. You are moving with it into the future, and what you do next is a cause.
